The Battle of Austerlitz. On December 2, 1805, near the town of Austerlitz in what is now the Czech Republic, Napoleon achieved one of his greatest tactical masterpieces. Called the Battle of the Three Emperors because Napoleon, Tsar Alexander the First, and Holy Roman Emperor Francis the Second all commanded forces on the field, it involved approximately 73,000 French troops facing 85,000 Austro-Russian forces. The Austro-Russian coalition sought to trap Napoleon, but he feigned weakness on his right flank to draw them south, then attacked their now-exposed center. Soult's corps smashed through the Austro-Russian center at the Pratzen Heights, splitting and routing the Allied army. Russian and Austrian cavalry reserves could not recover the day. Combined losses exceeded 26,000, with thousands captured. Weeks later, the Treaty of Pressburg forced Austria to cede territory and Italy to France and Bavaria, and it dissolved the Holy Roman Empire. The victory secured Napoleon's control of northern Europe and forced Britain to rely on naval and colonial power rather than finding Continental allies. Military academies still study this battle as a model of maneuver warfare and often cite it as the peak of Napoleonic tactical genius. The battle cemented French continental dominance and stands as Napoleon's greatest moment of tactical brilliance.
